output:
Kelechi Obi  
Croydon  

My dear Kelechi,

Yes, this is an actual letter. On paper, in an envelope, with a stamp. You said at my birthday that if I was serious, I should put it in writing, a proper letter and not a voice note, so here we are. Please respect the effort. If you’re reading this on the train, try not to laugh too loudly and disturb the other passengers.

I was serious.

When you started moaning about work again and I said you should come and teach maths, it wasn’t just the first thing that entered my mouth. Nine years as a quantity surveyor, and according to you, every day is the same spreadsheet wearing a slightly different shirt. You are bored to death. We have established this thoroughly. I wasn’t simply trying to bring that part of the conversation to an end, although that would have been a useful public service.

I suggested teaching because I genuinely think you could be very good at it.

You seem to have forgotten that you got an A in Further Maths and then tutored half our hostel in Moremi before exams. I have not forgotten. People who had been pretending to understand things all semester would appear with their notes and their confusion, and you would sit down and patiently take them through it again. You never made anybody feel stupid for asking. You just found another way of explaining it until something clicked.

That is not a small thing. In fact, apart from actually knowing your subject and being able to locate a working board pen, it may be most of the job.

You are still doing it now. Look at what you did with my nephew at Christmas. The boy was fighting fractions, and you used portions of jollof rice on plates to explain them. No speech, no drama, no “when I was your age”. You just taught him in a way that made sense to him. He still talks about it. Not just the rice, although obviously the rice was important. He talks about how you explained it.

You are patient, you are funny, and you don’t turn explaining something into an opportunity to prove you are the cleverest person in the room. Children would respond to that. Not every child, every day, because children are not a fan club, but they would know you were on their side.

And before you decide this is just me trying to recruit a friend because my school is short-staffed, let me be honest: we are short-staffed. I work in a school of about 1,100 children, and we have had a supply teacher covering two Year 9 maths groups since September. Those pupils need consistency. They need somebody who knows them, knows the subject and can stay long enough to see them improve. I’m not saying you should arrive tomorrow morning with a briefcase and save everybody. I’m saying the need is real. It is not an abstract teacher-shortage headline to me. It has names and faces.

One of those names is Damola. He’s in Year 11, and last month he finally understood simultaneous equations after three weeks of us working at them. When it clicked, he shouted, “Is that all??” and the whole class clapped. He was almost offended that the thing which had been tormenting him for weeks could suddenly look so straightforward.

I thought about that moment on my way home. Not because I expect an assembly in my honour, but because he had gone from deciding he simply couldn’t do it to realising that he could. That changes how a young person walks into the next lesson. It can change how they walk into an exam. Sometimes it changes what they believe about themselves.

And before you accuse me of making teaching sound like a film, no, the whole class does not clap every day. Most days, nobody claps. Somebody has forgotten their calculator, somebody else has lost their book, and the carefully planned activity that looked excellent on paper has died within four minutes.

So let me give you the bad parts properly, because I know you won’t believe the good parts otherwise.

Teaching is hard. The marking is endless until you learn how to manage it sensibly, and even then it can pile up. Behaviour some days is pure wahala. You will explain something clearly, check that everybody understands, and thirty seconds later someone will ask the exact question you have just answered. There are meetings, planning, parents, data and days when you get home with nothing sensible left to say. The holidays are substantial, but they are not all spent lying down; some of that time goes into planning, marking and recovering enough to become a human being again.

When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice during my first term. Twice. I sat in my car and questioned every decision that had brought me there. Not my most glamorous professional era, and I’m not hiding it from you.

But it got better. Not by magic, and not because the children suddenly became angels. I learned what to let go of, how to plan without trying to produce a masterpiece for every lesson, when to ask for help and how to stop treating one bad period as a verdict on my entire career. Some days are still difficult. The difference is that I now have enough good days, and enough evidence of progress, to know why I’m doing it.

You might try teaching and decide it isn’t for you. That is allowed. I don’t want you to exchange one unhappy working life for another simply because your friend wrote you a persuasive letter. But you cannot know from the outside, while bored at your current desk, that it would be worse.

We should also talk about money, because obviously you will ask, and obviously you should. The route I’m suggesting is the salaried training route. It lasts one year, and you are paid while you train. It starts in September 2027, so this is not me asking you to resign next Tuesday and begin contemplating your life in a staffroom by Friday.

The first year would mean a pay drop. I won’t pretend otherwise or hide it underneath talk about purpose. You have bills and responsibilities, and romance does not pay rent. Before you make any actual decision, we would sit down with the real figures and work out what is manageable. I will even let you build the spreadsheet. It may help you feel in control.

After training, pay increases as you progress. There is also the pension and the holidays. Those things matter, particularly when you are thinking beyond next month. They do not automatically make the finances easy, but they belong in the calculation.

As for being too old, abeg. You are 34, not 94. A woman in my department started teaching at 41, so you can stop constructing your midlife crisis before it has even arrived. You would bring nine years of professional experience with you: working under pressure, dealing with people, being precise, explaining complicated information and noticing when something doesn’t add up. None of that disappears because you change buildings.

I know quantity surveying is useful work. I am not starting a campaign against buildings, budgets or cost plans. But I do think you are wasting a part of yourself checking other people’s costings. The part that can sit with a confused hostel mate, or a child with a plate of jollof rice, and make something difficult feel possible.

On your last birthday, you said, “I just want to do something that matters before 40.” I’m not throwing that back at you to trap you. You weren’t asking me to reorganise your life, and being good at teaching doesn’t mean you owe teaching the rest of your life. I just haven’t forgotten that you said it. Neither have I forgotten the way you sounded.

So my actual request is much smaller than the speech you are probably preparing for.

Come to the open evening.

It is on Thursday 19 November 2026 at 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham. I can come with you. Applications for the September 2027 intake open soon, so this is the right time to gather information properly.

You don’t have to sign anything. You don’t have to apply. You certainly don’t have to announce a new chapter of your life on LinkedIn. Just come and ask blunt questions about the salary, workload, placements, behaviour support and what happens if somebody starts and hates it. Ask all the questions you would ask if somebody was trying to get you involved in a suspicious investment. I’ll sit with you while you ask them. I will attempt to keep quiet.

Afterwards, we can go and eat, and you can tell me every reason it isn’t for you. At least then they will be informed reasons. If your answer is still no, I’ll accept it. I may sulk briefly, but I’ll accept it.

When I said you should teach maths, I wasn’t trying to flatter you. I was picturing those two Year 9 groups, and all the Damolas who have decided maths is not for them, and thinking of the man who used to tutor half of Moremi without making anybody feel foolish.

That’s all. No preaching. Just one evening.

Think about it, guy. And when you’ve finished reading, text me. A voice note is also acceptable. I have used up my entire supply of formality.

Your guy,  
**[Your name]**
